concepts.name: If-then plans turn intentions into action
Choosing the next skill from lost-job evidence

questions.prompt: Your upkeep is three coding problems a week. Which schedule does the research on distributed practice support?

choices.text: All three on Sunday, in one three-hour block
One each on Monday, Wednesday and Friday
None for seven weeks, then 24 in week eight
Any schedule; only the total time spent matters

questions.explanation: Distributed practice means spreading study sessions out over time instead of massing them together. Dunlosky et al. (2013) rate it high utility. In the review by Cepeda et al. (2006) that they cite, 254 studies with over 14,000 participants, recall was 47% after spaced study against 37% after massed study. The total time can be the same; the spacing is what makes the difference.

sources.title: Improving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques: Promising Directions From Cognitive and Educational Psychology (Dunlosky et al., 2013, Psychological Science in the Public Interest 14(1))
sources.claim: Dunlosky et al. rate distributed practice high utility and report Cepeda et al. (2006), 254 studies with over 14,000 participants, where recall was 47% after spaced study versus 37% after massed study.

questions.prompt: In Bahrick's (1979) study, described by Dunlosky et al., relearning sessions were 0, 1 or 30 days apart. Which gave the best retention on a test 30 days later?

choices.text: 0 days apart: learning was fastest, so retention was best
1 day apart: it was best both during practice and at the final test
30 days apart: most forgetting between sessions, yet the best final retention
All three were about equal once learners reached the same level

questions.explanation: The 30-day group forgot the most between sessions and never reached the others' level during practice, yet it retained the most on the final test. Spaced beat massed, and a longer gap beat a shorter one. Harder practice is not a sign that it isn't working, which is why a weekly problem that feels rusty is doing its job.

sources.title: Improving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques: Promising Directions From Cognitive and Educational Psychology (Dunlosky et al., 2013, Psychological Science in the Public Interest 14(1))
sources.claim: In Bahrick (1979) as described by Dunlosky et al., the 30-day group forgot most between sessions and never reached the others' practice level, yet had the best retention on the final test 30 days later.

questions.prompt: Explain why spreading your weekly upkeep across the week beats one long session, even though the long session often feels more productive.

model_answer.summary: Spaced practice produces better long-term retention than massed practice with the same total time. Massed practice can do better on an immediate test, which is why it feels effective.
key_points: Dunlosky et al. (2013) rate distributed practice as high utility
Spaced study beats massed study on delayed tests (47% vs 37% recall across 254 studies in Cepeda et al., 2006)
Massed practice (cramming) can win on an immediate test, so it feels effective even though it fades faster
Some forgetting between sessions makes the next retrieval harder, and in Bahrick's study the widest gaps gave the best retention

questions.explanation: Interviews are delayed tests: the question comes weeks after you practised. A schedule that feels less fluent in the moment is the one that holds up then.

sources.title: Improving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques: Promising Directions From Cognitive and Educational Psychology (Dunlosky et al., 2013, Psychological Science in the Public Interest 14(1))
sources.claim: Dunlosky et al. rate distributed practice high utility, cite 47% vs 37% recall for spaced vs massed study across 254 studies, and describe Bahrick's 30-day lag giving the best retention despite most forgetting between sessions.

sources.title: Strengthening the Student Toolbox
sources.claim: Dunlosky notes massed practice feels easier and gives quick but temporary learning, while spaced practice gives more durable retention.

questions.prompt: In Rohrer and Taylor (2007), students practised either blocked (all problems of one kind, then the next kind) or interleaved (kinds mixed). What happened?

choices.text: Interleaved was better both during practice and on the test a week later
Blocked was better both during practice and on the test a week later
The two schedules gave about the same results
Blocked was better during practice; interleaved was far better a week later

questions.explanation: Dunlosky et al. describe this as the typical interleaving effect: blocked practice looked better during the practice sessions, but the advantage reversed on the delayed test, where interleaving raised accuracy by 43%. Judging a schedule by how practice feels would pick the wrong one.

sources.title: Improving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques: Promising Directions From Cognitive and Educational Psychology (Dunlosky et al., 2013, Psychological Science in the Public Interest 14(1))
sources.claim: Dunlosky et al. describe Rohrer and Taylor (2007) as a typical interleaving effect: blocked practice did better during practice, but interleaved practice boosted accuracy on the delayed test by 43%.

questions.prompt: Why mix patterns in your three weekly problems (say, a sliding window, a graph and a heap) instead of doing three of the same pattern?

choices.text: It trains you to spot which method a problem needs; interviews don't name the pattern
It makes each session feel easier and more fluent
Dunlosky et al. rate it the most effective technique, above practice testing
It lets you skip redoing the problems you got wrong

questions.explanation: The explanation Dunlosky et al. give is that interleaving makes you practise choosing the right solution method for each problem, which blocked practice skips because the method is obvious from the block. In an interview, recognising the pattern is half the problem. They rate interleaving moderate utility, below practice testing and distributed practice, and it tends to feel harder, not easier.

sources.title: Improving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques: Promising Directions From Cognitive and Educational Psychology (Dunlosky et al., 2013, Psychological Science in the Public Interest 14(1))
sources.claim: Dunlosky et al. explain that interleaving gives practice at identifying which solution method a problem needs, and rate interleaved practice moderate utility, below practice testing and distributed practice.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an implementation intention in Gollwitzer and Sheeran's sense?

choices.text: "I will do much more coding practice over the next eight weeks."
"My goal is 24 problems and eight build-log posts by the end of week eight."
"If it is Monday, Wednesday or Friday at 7 a.m., then I open NeetCode and do one problem."
"I intend to become strong at dynamic programming."

questions.explanation: An implementation intention is an if-then plan that links a situation (when and where) to a specific response: "If situation Y occurs, then I will do Z." The other three are goal intentions. They say what you want to do or achieve, but not when, where or how, and that gap is where plans fail.

sources.title: Implementation Intentions (Gollwitzer and Sheeran)
sources.publisher: National Cancer Institute (Division of Cancer Control and Population Sciences)
sources.claim: Gollwitzer and Sheeran define implementation intentions as if-then plans linking a situational cue to a response ("If situation Y is encountered, then I will initiate behavior Z"), unlike goal intentions that only state what one intends to achieve.

questions.prompt: This Lesson's exercise is to put the first week of your plan in your calendar. Explain, using the research on implementation intentions, why that step matters.

model_answer.summary: Goal intentions often don't turn into action. An if-then plan tied to a specific time and place, which a calendar entry gives you, raises goal attainment with a medium-to-large effect.
key_points: A goal intention states what you want to achieve; an implementation intention adds when, where and how, as an if-then plan
Strong goal intentions still often fail to become action (the intention-behaviour gap)
Across 94 studies, forming implementation intentions had a medium-to-large effect on goal attainment (d = .65)
The calendar entry is the situational cue (the "if"), so you no longer have to decide when to act
If-then plans work best when the underlying goal is strong and active

questions.explanation: Gollwitzer and Sheeran explain that forming the plan links the cue to the response, so starting becomes close to automatic. A plan in your head with no set time has no cue to trigger it.

sources.title: Implementation Intentions (Gollwitzer and Sheeran)
sources.publisher: National Cancer Institute (Division of Cancer Control and Population Sciences)
sources.claim: Gollwitzer and Sheeran report that strong goal intentions often fail to become action, and that forming implementation intentions had a medium-to-large effect on goal attainment across 94 studies (d = .65).

questions.prompt: According to Gollwitzer and Sheeran, when do if-then plans have the strongest effect?

choices.text: When the plan leaves the time open so it can adapt to your week
When the underlying goal intention is strong and active
When someone else, such as a manager, set the goal
When one plan covers several unrelated goals at once

questions.explanation: They report that strong implementation-intention effects appeared mainly when the underlying goal intention was strong and activated. They also cite evidence that if-then plans helped more with personal projects that matched people's own interests than with ones driven by outside pressure. A plan with an open time has no "if" to trigger it.

sources.title: Implementation Intentions (Gollwitzer and Sheeran)
sources.publisher: National Cancer Institute (Division of Cancer Control and Population Sciences)
sources.claim: Gollwitzer and Sheeran report strong implementation-intention effects mainly when the underlying goal intention was strong and activated, and larger benefits for personal projects consistent with one's own interests than for externally pressured ones.

questions.prompt: Over four weeks you lost 8 roles. For each, you noted the requirement you lacked: Kubernetes in 5, fine-tuning in 2, voice agents in 1. Which next skill does this Lesson's rule (pick based on the jobs you are losing) point to?

choices.text: Voice agents, because they are the newest area
Fine-tuning, because it is the most advanced of the three
All three at once, a few hours each
Kubernetes, because it is the gap in most of the lost roles

questions.explanation: The rule is evidence-based: count what you lacked in the roles you lost, and fix the most frequent gap. Kubernetes accounts for 5 of the 8. Hype and difficulty aren't in the rule. Splitting eight weeks across three skills also leaves too little spaced practice on any one of them to show in an interview.

sources.title: Practical guide to writing FAANG-ready software engineer resumes | Tech Interview Handbook
sources.claim: The handbook advises analysing job descriptions to identify the must-have skills, which supports choosing the skill most often required by the target roles (here 5 of 8).

sources.title: Technical Interview Guide for Busy Engineers | Tech Interview Handbook
sources.claim: The handbook focuses preparation on the minimum you need to know rather than covering everything.

questions.prompt: An interviewer asks: "What are you learning next, and why?" Explain how you chose, using the jobs you have been losing, and how you will know it was the right choice.

model_answer.summary: I recorded the requirement I lacked for each role I lost and picked the most frequent one. I practise it on a fixed schedule and check the tally again after eight weeks.
key_points: For each lost role, record the stage you lost at and the requirement you lacked
Count the gaps and pick the single most frequent one, not the most fashionable
Tie it to the target roles: say how many of the posts you are applying to ask for it
Plan spaced, scheduled practice on that one skill, with a visible output such as a project or a build-log post
Re-count after eight weeks, and switch if the losses now come from a different gap

questions.explanation: A good answer gives a reason grounded in evidence and names a way to check it. "I read that X is hot" is weaker than "5 of the 8 roles I lost needed X, and here is what I've built with it so far".

sources.title: Practical guide to writing FAANG-ready software engineer resumes | Tech Interview Handbook
sources.claim: The handbook advises analysing target job descriptions to identify must-have skills and experiences.

questions.prompt: Which findings support spreading upkeep practice across the week? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Massed practice is always superior on delayed retention tests.
Distributed practice was rated high utility in the cited review.
Spaced study can improve delayed recall compared with massed study.
Immediate ease of practice does not prove durable retention.
Spaced practice means completing all repetitions in one uninterrupted sitting.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect: the review reports a delayed-recall advantage from spacing. B: Correct: distributed practice is a strongly supported learning technique. C: Correct: the cited synthesis reports better spaced-study recall. D: Correct: massed practice can feel fluent but fade faster. E: Incorrect: distributed practice separates sessions over time.

questions.prompt: Which statements describe effective implementation intentions? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Use an if-then plan linking a situational cue to a specific action.
Treat a strong wish to improve as a guarantee that practice will happen.
Specify when and how you will act on an active goal.
Implementation intentions replace the need to care about the underlying goal.
A planned calendar cue can identify when the practice action should begin.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: cue-response links are the defining form of these plans. B: Incorrect: even strong goal intentions can fail to become action. C: Correct: concrete plans help translate goal intentions into behavior. D: Incorrect: effects are stronger with strong activated goal intentions. E: Correct: a time or situation can serve as the if condition for starting.

questions.prompt: Which practices support selecting and retaining a role-relevant next skill? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Choose only the most fashionable skill without checking target job requirements.
Analyze target postings for required skills and experience.
Cram all study into one sitting because spacing weakens retention.
Match practice priorities to the requirements your target roles actually state.
Distribute learning sessions over time for longer-term retention.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect: job-description evidence identifies relevant skill needs. B: Correct: the resume handbook recommends analyzing must-have requirements. C: Incorrect: distributed practice supports stronger retention than massed study. D: Correct: role requirements provide a concrete basis for prioritizing skills. E: Correct: the learning review rates distributed practice high utility.
